design_detail: Series of operant experiments in rats (PLoS ONE 2007, e698). Male Wistar rats with jugular catheters chose, in a discrete-trials procedure (12 trials a day, 10 minutes apart: 4 forced sampling trials, always in the order cocaine lever, saccharin lever, cocaine lever, saccharin lever, an order chosen to prevent drug-induced taste aversion, then 8 free choices, for 15 days), between a lever that delivered one intravenous cocaine infusion and a lever that gave 20 s of access to 0.2% saccharin water. Three between-group conditions (only cocaine rewarded, only saccharin rewarded, both rewarded) were followed by within-animal tests of cocaine dose, saccharin delay and response cost, tests with water, no fluid and 4% sucrose as the alternative, a reversal test in rats that had first learned to prefer cocaine, and tests after 18 days of extended (6 h a day) cocaine access and during cocaine intoxication. A secondary synthesis read ventral striatal dopamine values off the figures of 18 rat microdialysis papers. Every finding on this card is in rats; nothing was measured in people.
can_establish: That under this discrete-trials procedure, male Wistar rats with no previous experience of refined sugar almost all chose a saccharin (or sucrose) drink over an intravenous cocaine infusion, and kept doing so across the cocaine doses, delays and response costs tested, after a period of escalating cocaine intake and while under the influence of cocaine.
cannot_establish: That sweet taste outweighs cocaine for people, for female rats or under other procedures (longer access, other spacing of trials, other alternatives); that the escalated rats were addicted in any sense beyond escalated intake; or anything about sugar addiction or drug use in human societies, which the authors offer as speculation.

sample.recruitment: Laboratory animals: naive young adult male Wistar rats from Charles River, France; housed 2 or 3 per cage under a reversed 12-h light cycle with food and water freely available; standard chow without added synthetic or refined sugar; tested in the dark phase (Materials and Methods › Subjects).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Rats that completed fewer than 50% of the 8 daily choice trials after 15 days were excluded: 20 of 132, 16 in the cocaine-only condition and 4 in the both-rewarded condition (Materials and Methods › Data analysis).
sample.demographics: Male only; 221–276 g at the start; no previous operant training and no experience of refined sugar or artificial sweetener.
sample.attrition: 20 of 132 rats (15%) excluded, unevenly across conditions (16 cocaine-only, 4 both-rewarded, none saccharin-only). The paper does not say whether the printed group sizes (30, 9 and 43) count rats before or after exclusion; the degrees of freedom of the main analysis, F(28,1106), fit 82 analysed rats in the three conditions, in which case about a third of the cocaine-only condition (16 of 46) was excluded (editors' calculation).
sample.selection_effects: One strain, one sex, one supplier; rats were not food- or water-restricted. Exclusion removed rats that did not engage with the task, mostly in the cocaine-only condition. How rats were assigned to conditions and chosen for the later subgroup tests is not described, and the named groups cannot all be independent (see reporting issues).

exposure.measurement: Intravenous self-administration through a jugular catheter (patency checked with etomidate when needed), each infusion triggered by a lever press and recorded by the apparatus; cocaine hydrochloride from a pharmaceutical supplier (Materials and Methods › Surgery; Drugs).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions in rats, not applicable to people: cocaine hydrochloride IV, 0.25 mg per infusion over 4 s (dose as salt) in the main procedure; 0.25, 0.75 and 1.5 mg per infusion in a dose test, with the inter-trial interval lengthened with dose (10, 16.4 and 23.1 min); extended-access group 6 h a day for 18 days (0.25 mg per infusion in the first hour, 0.75 mg after); intoxication group 1 h of cocaine-only access before each day's choices. In the both-rewarded condition rats took about 3 infusions a day, sampling included (Discussion, 2nd paragraph). Alternative reward: 20 s of access to 0.2% sodium saccharin (at most 0.3 ml) or 4% sucrose.
exposure.polysubstance: None: one drug, and rats had no other drug exposure.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable: cocaine was available during testing; the intoxication group chose immediately after 1 h of cocaine access.

comparison.controls: Between groups: rats for which only the saccharin lever (N=9) or only the cocaine lever (N=30) was rewarded. Within animals: water and no fluid as the alternative (same 10 rats), and 4% sucrose (a separate 10 rats). The reversal and escalation groups were compared with the initially drug-naive both-rewarded rats.
comparison.matching: Same strain, sex, supplier and weight range; all three conditions were indifferent between the levers on day 1 (Results, 2nd paragraph).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Individual differences that could predict choice (for example sweet preference or sensitivity to cocaine) were not measured before allocation.

outcomes.instruments: Lever choice (share of completed choice trials on each lever, plotted against an indifference level of 0), recorded automatically; latencies to sample and to choose; locomotion by infrared beam crossings for 10 min after the first cocaine infusion of the day (sensitization); daily cocaine intake during extended access; delay to onset of cocaine effects timed by observation (12 rats); ventral striatal dopamine values read off published figures (18 papers).
outcomes.validity_norms: Discrete-trials choice between a drug and an alternative is an established procedure, mostly from monkey studies that the authors discuss. An individual rat was counted as preferring the cocaine lever when it chose it on more than 60% of trials over the last 3 days (Results, 7th paragraph).
outcomes.operationalization: Preference: choosing one lever on more than 50% of completed choices (group means tested against indifference) or, for individual rats, more than 60% over the last 3 stable days. Addiction: inferred from escalation of intake over 18 days of 6-h access; compulsive use despite negative consequences and relapse were not tested in this paper.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None across experiments; Fisher's LSD tests after ANOVA within experiments. The count of 18 is the editors' count of distinct tests reported in the Results.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Choice, latencies and locomotion were recorded automatically. The onset delay of cocaine effects was timed by an observer who knew cocaine had been given; blinding is not reported for any procedure.

analysis.effect_sizes: No standardized effect sizes; F, t and z tests with significance thresholds, and group means shown only in figures (images, not viewable in this reading). Printed values: Condition×Day F(28,1106)=8.71, P<0.01; both-rewarded vs saccharin-only F(14,700)=0.41, NS; choice latency 14.5±5.0 vs 6.5±2.4 s, t(50)<1; sampling latency cocaine lever 48.5±10.2 vs saccharin lever 5.6±1.7 s, F(1,42)=17.44, P<0.01; sensitization Day×Intervals F(40,1160)=5.06 (cocaine-only) and F(40,1680)=6.57 (both-rewarded), P<0.01; first both-rewarded day in rats trained with saccharin only, Group×Intervals F(20,1000)=1.66, P<0.05; dose: locomotion F(2,20)=18.77, P<0.01, choice F(2,20)=0.07, NS; saccharin delay F(3,30)=6.58, P<0.01; response cost F(2,18)=8.04, P<0.01; escalation from 7.34±2.50 to 26.04±1.21 mg/day, F(16,160)=15.98, P<0.01; rats preferring cocaine 2.3% (initially naive), 8.3% (after reversal), 0.0% (after escalation), z<1.96 for both comparisons; escalated rats' sampling latencies 15.6±8.1 vs 4.0±0.8 s, F(1,10)=2.06, NS. Degrees of freedom match the stated group sizes throughout (editors' check).
analysis.selective_reporting: Most results appear only as figure means with significance marks; individual data are shown for 3 representative rats only. The 94% in the abstract does not appear in the results (see reporting issues).
analysis.power: Not reported; groups of 9 to 43 rats, subgroups of 10 or 11.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In male Wistar rats under one discrete-trials procedure (8 choices a day, 10 minutes apart; about 3 cocaine infusions a day when both rewards were available), almost every rat chose the sweet drink over intravenous cocaine, and this held across the doses, delays and costs tested, after reversal, after escalated intake and during intoxication; the same rats preferred cocaine to plain water.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says the findings “clearly demonstrate” that intense sweetness can surpass cocaine reward even in drug-sensitized and -addicted individuals; here addiction rests on escalated intake after 18 days of extended access, without tests of compulsive use or relapse. The extensions to people (that sugar-rich diets could lead to addiction through supranormal stimulation of sweet receptors, and that widespread sugar may shield modern societies against the spread of drug addiction) are labelled as speculation in the abstract and Discussion, 6th paragraph; no human data were collected. The conclusion that the reward value of cocaine is “bounded” is tied to this procedure: the authors note that monkeys in earlier studies preferred high cocaine doses over food, in one study over a sucrose pellet, and that a species difference cannot be ruled out (Discussion, 3rd paragraph).

timeline.event: Rhesus monkeys chose intravenous cocaine over food in a choice procedure (Aigner & Balster, 1978, as described in this paper); animal study.
Rhesus monkeys preferred the highest cocaine dose over a 1-g sucrose pellet (Woolverton & Balster, 1979, as described in this paper); animal study, contrary to the rat result.

Rats: concurrently available sweetened water (saccharin plus glucose) prevented acquisition or reduced maintenance of low-dose cocaine self-administration (Carroll et al., 1989; and Carroll & Lac, 1993, as described in this paper).

Human inpatient laboratory study: choice between smoked cocaine and a money or merchandise voucher in six participants (Hart et al., 2000; on the General list, not yet appraised); a study in people, kept apart from the rat findings
Rats: social interaction as the alternative to drugs (Venniro et al., 2018; on the General list, not yet appraised).
Critical history of the Rat Park experiments and how animal environment studies shaped accounts of addiction (Gage & Sumnall, 2019; not yet appraised)

replication.where_it_stands: Within this paper the rats' preference held across many manipulations, but in one strain, one sex and one procedure. Earlier monkey choice studies found the opposite preference, as the authors discuss, and the General list notes that later choice studies show the outcome depends on the drug, the procedure and the alternative (Kearns, 2023; Banks & Negus, 2017; not yet appraised). It is evidence about how a non-drug alternative competes with cocaine in rats, not evidence about people.

funding.funder: Université Victor-Segalen Bordeaux 2, the French Research Council (CNRS), the Conseil Régional Aquitaine, the National Research Agency (ANR) and the Fondation pour la Recherche Médicale (FRM) (Footnotes › Funding).
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors have declared that no competing interests exist (Footnotes › Competing Interests).
funding.affiliations_note: University Bordeaux 2 and Bordeaux 1, CNRS UMR 5227. The extended-access escalation model and the view that escalated rats show signs of addiction come from the senior author's earlier work (Ahmed & Koob, 1998; Ahmed et al., 2002, as cited). Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: For rats: choice experiments in females and males of several strains, with randomized allocation and order, blinded handling, a pre-registered protocol and full reporting of excluded animals, varying trial spacing, access duration and the kind of alternative. For people, a different design entirely: laboratory and field studies of how available non-drug rewards change cocaine choice (as in contingency management), which no rat study can answer.

domains.note: No random component is described for allocating rats to the three conditions, and the within-animal tests ran in a fixed ascending order (cocaine 0.25, 0.75, 1.5 mg; saccharin delay 0, 6, 12, 18 s; cost 2, 4, 8 presses; no fluid, water, saccharin), so order and practice effects are confounded with the manipulated variable.
Same strain, sex, supplier and weight range; all conditions indifferent between the levers on day 1. Per-group weights are not reported.
Rats were housed 2 or 3 per cage and tested in 12 chambers; how cages and chambers were assigned is not reported.

domains.domain: 5. Blinding of caregivers and investigators (performance bias)
domains.note: Not reported; contingencies were programmed, but handling and catheter care by staff who knew each rat's condition cannot be excluded.
Choice was recorded for every rat, but the subgroups tested for dose, delay, cost, water and sucrose were drawn from the trained rats without a stated method of selection.
The main outcomes (lever choice, latencies, beam-break locomotion) were recorded automatically. The one observer-timed measure, the onset delay of cocaine effects, was not blinded but is not central.

20 of 132 rats were excluded for completing fewer than half the choice trials, a reason linked to the outcome, unevenly across conditions (16 cocaine-only, 4 both-rewarded, none saccharin-only). The main both-rewarded result lost 4 rats and is unlikely to change; comparisons with the cocaine-only condition are more exposed.
No protocol (none would be expected in 2007); every experiment named in the Methods is reported, mostly as figure means; the abstract's 94% cannot be traced in the Results.
Rats were reused across later experiments without saying which, so earlier tests may carry over; the dopamine synthesis read values off figures from 18 papers chosen without stated criteria.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: SYRCLE defines no overall judgment; the overall here is the editors' summary, set to the most severe judgment among the items that bear on the main result. The core outcome was recorded automatically, and the preference is large and consistent across experiments, which limits detection bias. But no random allocation is described, the dose, delay and cost tests ran in fixed ascending order, 15% of rats (most of them in the cocaine-only condition) were excluded for not engaging with the task, and the use of rats across experiments is not reported. The paper may be cited for what male Wistar rats did in this procedure, labelled as an animal finding; it may not be cited for sweet or cocaine preference in people, for addiction in people, or for a general ranking of rewards.

preclinical.species_strain_sex: Rat; Wistar; male only; young adults of 221–276 g at the start (Charles River, France); N=132, of whom 20 were excluded.
preclinical.dose_route_schedule: Cocaine hydrochloride, intravenous through a jugular catheter, 0.25 mg per infusion over 4 s in the main procedure (0.75 and 1.5 mg in a dose test; 0.75 mg after the first hour in the extended-access phase); 12 trials a day spaced 10 minutes apart (4 forced, 8 choices) for 15 days; extended access 6 h a day for 18 days in one group; 1 h of cocaine-only access before choices in another. Alternative: 20 s of 0.2% saccharin (or 4% sucrose) drinking.
preclinical.human_equivalent_dose_basis: None given: doses are stated per infusion in mg of salt, not per kg, and the authors make no human-equivalent statement. None is calculated here.
preclinical.resembles_human_use: Partly. Intravenous self-administration is a standard model of cocaine taking, and the extended-access group models escalating intake. But the main procedure allowed 8 choices a day spaced 10 minutes apart (about 3 infusions a day when saccharin was available, against about 30 when rats take cocaine freely over the same time), offered a small, immediate sweet drink as the only alternative, used rats that were neither food- nor water-restricted and had never tasted refined sugar, and studied males only. People's choices involve delayed, social, economic and legal consequences that the procedure does not model.

key_findings.finding: Rats (male Wistar, drug-naive, no previous refined sugar): offered one intravenous cocaine infusion (0.25 mg) or 20 s of 0.2% saccharin water on each choice trial (both levers rewarded, N=43), the group preferred saccharin from the 2nd day of testing, as quickly as rats for which only saccharin was available (N=9; both-rewarded vs saccharin-only F(14,700)=0.41, NS). Rats with only the cocaine lever rewarded (N=30) came to prefer it from day 9 (significant from day 11). Condition×Day F(28,1106)=8.71, P<0.01.
key_findings.note: The Discussion (5th paragraph) says instead that the both-rewarded rats reached a reliable saccharin preference more rapidly than the saccharin-only rats (day 2 against day 7); the formal comparison found no difference (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Rats: once behaviour was stable, choosing saccharin took as long in the both-rewarded condition (14.5±5.0 s) as in the saccharin-only condition (6.5±2.4 s; t(50)<1). Rats sampled the cocaine lever almost every time from day 7 but pressed it more slowly than the saccharin lever during sampling (48.5±10.2 vs 5.6±1.7 s; F(1,42)=17.44, P<0.01).

Rats preferred cocaine over plain water, so the saccharin preference was not explained by thirst (the same 10 rats were tested with no fluid, water and saccharin, in that order); a separate 10 rats preferred 4% sucrose over cocaine as others preferred saccharin.
key_findings.note: Group values are shown only in Figure 2, an image not viewable in this reading.

key_findings.finding: Rats: the few cocaine infusions taken in the both-rewarded condition produced locomotor sensitization similar to that in the cocaine-only condition (Day×Intervals F(40,1680)=6.57 and F(40,1160)=5.06, P<0.01); rats first trained with saccharin only were less sensitized on their first both-rewarded day (Group×Intervals F(20,1000)=1.66, P<0.05).

Rats (subgroups of the both-rewarded group): raising the cocaine dose to 0.75 and 1.5 mg per infusion increased locomotion (F(2,20)=18.77, P<0.01) but not cocaine choice (F(2,20)=0.07, NS; N=11); delaying the saccharin by up to 18 s slightly reduced saccharin choice without reversing the preference (F(3,30)=6.58, P<0.01; N=11); raising the cost from 2 to 8 presses increased the saccharin preference (F(2,18)=8.04, P<0.01; N=10).

Rats that had first learned to prefer the cocaine lever (cocaine-only condition, N=24) switched to saccharin once both levers were rewarded; 8.3% of them still preferred cocaine (more than 60% cocaine choices over the last 3 days), against 2.3% of initially drug-naive rats (z<1.96).

Rats given 6 h of cocaine access a day for 18 days (N=11) escalated intake from 7.34±2.50 to 26.04±1.21 mg/day (F(16,160)=15.98, P<0.01) and then, within 10 days of choice, preferred saccharin; none preferred cocaine (0.0% vs 2.3% of initially naive rats); the preference held across cocaine doses, with a small decrease at the highest dose.
key_findings.locator: Results, 7th paragraph; Figure 5b and insert; Materials and Methods › Induction of cocaine intake escalation

key_findings.finding: Rats that self-administered cocaine for 1 h before each choice session (N=10) still developed a robust saccharin preference, switching abruptly from the cocaine lever to the saccharin lever when the choices began (3 representative rats shown).
key_findings.locator: Results, 7th paragraph; Figure 5c–e; Materials and Methods › Choice during cocaine intoxication

key_findings.finding: Rats: the preference was not exclusive. In the both-rewarded condition rats chose cocaine on about 15.6% of choices on average (range across experiments 7–23%), about 3 infusions a day with sampling, against about 30 infusions that rats take freely over the same period; in the saccharin-only condition they pressed the unrewarded cocaine lever on 8.3% of choices.

Rats, secondary synthesis: from the figures of 18 rat microdialysis papers found through Medline, the authors report that intravenous cocaine self-administration raised ventral striatal dopamine much more than sucrose or saccharin drinking, and argue that dopamine release alone does not explain the choice.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 4th paragraph; Figure 6; Materials and Methods › Meta-analysis
key_findings.note: Values only in Figure 6 (not viewable); papers selected by content and relevance without stated criteria, values estimated from published figures.

key_findings.finding: The authors note that in earlier discrete-trials studies most monkeys preferred high doses of intravenous cocaine over food, in one study over a 1-g sucrose pellet, and give possible reasons (sweet drink vs dry food, effort required, amount of the alternative, a species difference).

No measurement in people. The extension to human diets and drug use (sugar-rich diets as supernormal stimuli that could lead to addiction; widespread sugar as a possible shield against the spread of drug addiction) is offered by the authors as speculation.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says 94% of rats preferred saccharin; no 94% appears in the Results, which give the share of rats preferring cocaine by a more-than-60% criterion (2.3% of initially naive, 8.3% after reversal, 0.0% after escalation) and an average of 15.6% cocaine choices.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML: Abstract; Results, 7th paragraph; Discussion, 2nd paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The headline figure cannot be traced: which groups and which criterion it uses are not stated. Editors' arithmetic: the three groups with stated percentages hold 1 of 43, 2 of 24 and 0 of 11 rats preferring cocaine, 3 of 78 in all, so 96% did not; only the two drug-experienced groups together (2 of 35) would round to 94%, and the paper does not say that this is its basis.

reporting_issues.issue: Group sizes named in the text (30, 9 and 43 in the three conditions, 11 escalated, 10 intoxicated, and two groups of 10 in Figure 2) add up to 123 if the Figure 2 groups were separate rats, more than the 112 left after 20 exclusions; if they were drawn from the cocaine-only and both-rewarded conditions, as the Results' 1st paragraph implies (those conditions held more rats because the dose, delay, effort, reversal, calorie and thirst experiments were run in them), the named independent groups (30, 9, 43, 11 and 10) add up to 103, fewer than 112. Subgroups for dose (11), delay (11), cost (10), sucrose and water were drawn from the trained rats, and the text implies rats served in several experiments, but which rats did what is not reported.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML: Results, 1st, 4th, 6th and 7th paragraphs; Figure 2 legend; Materials and Methods › Subjects and Data analysis
reporting_issues.consequence: The number of independent animals behind each conclusion, and what each had experienced before later tests, cannot be reconstructed; carry-over between experiments is possible.

reporting_issues.issue: It is not stated whether the 20 exclusions (16 cocaine-only, 4 both-rewarded) come before or after the printed group sizes, but the degrees of freedom of every test that names its groups match the printed sizes (main ANOVA 82 rats; F(14,700), t(50) and F(20,1000) 52; F(40,1160) 30; F(40,1680) 43), so these are the sizes after exclusion: 16 of 46 cocaine-only rats (35%) against 4 of 47 both-rewarded rats (8.5%) were excluded for not completing choice trials (editors' arithmetic).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML: Materials and Methods › Data analysis; Results, 2nd paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The comparison of how quickly rats came to prefer cocaine or saccharin rests on the rats that engaged with the task; rats that rarely chose were removed mostly from the cocaine-only condition.

reporting_issues.issue: The extended-access phase lasted 18 days in the Methods but "3 weeks" in the Results; the ANOVA of daily intake (F(16,160)) implies 17 analysed sessions.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML: Results, 7th paragraph; Materials and Methods › Induction of cocaine intake escalation
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor: the length of the escalation phase is uncertain by a few days.

reporting_issues.issue: The Results (3rd paragraph) say the both-rewarded rats acquired the saccharin preference as quickly as the saccharin-only rats, in line with the formal comparison (F(14,700)=0.41, NS; 2nd paragraph), but the Discussion (5th paragraph) says they did so more rapidly (day 2 against day 7) and explains the difference by cocaine's ambivalent effects.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML: Results, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs; Discussion, 5th paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor. The days on which each group's preference first reached significance are not a test of a difference; the formal comparison found none, so the Discussion explains a difference the data do not show.
